So take warning, O people of insight.﴾ ﴿Had God not decreed exile for them, He would have punished them in this world, and in the Hereafter they will have the punishment of the Fire.﴾ ﴿That is because they opposed God and His Messenger. Whoever opposes God, indeed God is severe in punishment.﴾ ﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down, or whatever you left standing on their roots, it was by God's permission, and so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿And whatever God gave His Messenger from them, you did not spur horse or camel for it. But God gives His messengers power over whom He wills, and God is capable of everything.﴾ ﴿Whatever God gave His Messenger from the people of the towns belongs to God, to the Messenger, to the near kin, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer, so that it does not circulate only among the rich among you. Take what the Messenger gives you, and abstain from what he forbids you. And fear God; indeed God is severe in punishment.﴾

(p-241) [The same verses are repeated here in full, as above, with the same translation.]

(p-242) This surah is Medinan. It was said that it was revealed concerning the Banu al-Nadir, and it is counted among the Medinan surahs because of their proximity to Medina. The Banu al-Nadir had made a treaty with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that they would neither be against him nor with him. When he prevailed at Badr, they said: "This is the Prophet whom the Torah describes; his banner is never turned back." But when the Muslims were defeated at Uhud, they grew doubtful and broke the covenant. Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf went out with forty riders to Mecca, and they made an alliance with Quraysh at the Ka'bah. Gabriel informed the Messenger (ﷺ) of this, and he ordered the killing of Ka'b. Muhammad ibn Maslamah killed him by stealth (ghilah, meaning killing someone secretly by ambush), and he was his foster brother. The Prophet (ﷺ) had also discovered treachery from them when he went to them regarding the blood-money of the two Muslims whom 'Amr ibn Umayyah al-Damri had killed on his way back from the well of Ma'unah. They then plotted to drop a stone on the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but God protected him.

When Ka'b was killed, peace and blessings be upon him ordered a march against the Banu al-Nadir, who were in a village called al-Zuhrah. They set out, and he (peace and blessings be upon him) was riding a donkey with a halter of palm fiber. They found them wailing over Ka'b, and they said: "Let us weep for our griefs, then give your command." He said: "Leave the city." They replied: "Death is nearer to us than that," and they called out for war. It was also said that they asked him for a delay of ten days to prepare for departure. The hypocrite 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions secretly sent word: "Do not leave the fortress. If they fight you, we are with you and will surely support you, and if you are expelled, we will certainly leave with you." So they fortified the alleys and secured them. Then they agreed to betray the Messenger of God (ﷺ). They said: "Go out with thirty of your companions, and thirty of ours will go out to listen to you. If they believe you, we will all believe." He did so. They then said: "How can we understand when we are sixty? Go out with three, and three of our scholars will come out to you." They agreed, but they concealed daggers and intended to assassinate him. A woman among them who was a sincere advisor sent word to her brother, who was a Muslim, and told him what they intended. He hurried to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and whispered to him their plan before the Messenger reached them.

The next day, he came upon them with the battalions and besieged them for twenty-one nights. God cast terror into their hearts, and they despaired of the support of the hypocrites. They asked for peace, but he refused anything except exile, on the condition that each three of them could load one camel with whatever goods they wished. They went to Syria, to Ariha and Adhruʿat, except for two households of them, the family of Abu al-Haqiq and the family of Huyayy ibn Akhtab, who joined Khaybar. Some joined al-Hirah. He seized their wealth and weapons, and he found fifty coats of mail, fifty helmets, and three hundred and forty swords. Ibn Ubayy had told them: "I have two thousand men from my people and others with me, and Qurayzah and your allies from Ghatafan will support you." When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came against them, Qurayzah withdrew from them, and Ibn Ubayy and their allies from Ghatafan forsook them.

Its connection with what precedes it: when He mentioned the condition of the hypocrites and the Jews and how some of them became allies of others, He also mentioned what befell the Jews of the wrath of God upon them, their exile, and God's empowering of His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, over those who opposed God and His Messenger, sought to betray the Messenger, and openly showed enmity by their alliance with Quraysh.

The discussion of the glorification of inanimate things has already passed, which is covered by the general term "mā" (whatever).

﴿From the People of the Book﴾ [al-Hashr 11]: they are Qurayzah. They were a great tribe, comparable in rank and status to the Banu al-Nadir. They are also called "the two priests" (al-Kahinan), because they were descendants of the priest Kahin ibn Harun. They settled near Medina during the trials of the Children of Israel, awaiting Muhammad (ﷺ). What happened to them is what God recounted in His Book.

﴿From their homes﴾ [al-Hashr 8]: this is connected to akhraja (He expelled). ﴿From the People of the Book﴾ [al-Hashr 11] is connected to an omitted element, meaning "being among the People of the Book." The attribution of the homes to them is correct, because they were in a desert with no settlement, so they built and established themselves there.

The lam in ﴿at the first gathering﴾ [al-Hashr 2] is connected to akhraja. It is the lam of time, like His saying: ﴿at the decline of the sun﴾ [al-Isra 78], and the meaning is: at the first gathering. The hashr (gathering) is the assembling of people in order to direct them toward a certain place. The majority hold that those who were expelled were the Banu al-Nadir. al-Hasan said: they were the Banu Qurayzah. This was refuted on the grounds that the Banu Qurayzah were neither gathered nor exiled but were killed, and that this gathering refers to the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir. It was also said (p-243) that the gathering was the Messenger of God (ﷺ) assembling the battalions to fight them, and this was the first gathering from him against them and the first fighting he waged against them. The word "first" implies a "second," so it was said: the first gathering was their assembly for exile, and the second was the gathering of 'Umar against the people of Khaybar and their exile. The peace and blessings of God be upon him had informed of the exile of the people of Khaybar when he said: "Two religions shall not remain together in one jazirah." al-Hasan said: he meant the gathering of the Resurrection, meaning this is its first part, and rising from the graves is its last part. ʿIkrimah and al-Zuhri said: the meaning is that the first is the place of the gathering, which is Syria. In a hadith, he (peace and blessings be upon him) said to the Banu al-Nadir: "Leave," and they said: "To where?" He said: "To the land of the gathering." It was also said: the second is a fire that gathers people from east to west. This exile took place at the beginning of Islam, but now it has been abrogated (naskh, meaning the cancellation of a ruling by a later revealed ruling), so there must be killing, enslavement, or the imposition of the jizya (poll tax).

﴿You did not think they would leave﴾ [al-Hashr 2], because of the greatness of their affair, their strength, their power, the solidity of their fortresses, and the abundance of their numbers and equipment.

﴿And they thought that their fortresses would protect them from God's punishment and might.﴾ Since the thought of the believers is negated here, it is treated as the negation of hope and expectation, so it governs *an* (that), the particle that puts the verb into the subjunctive (*al-nasiba*), just as hope and expectation do. Since the Jews' thought was very strong, nearly reaching the level of knowledge, it governed *anna* (that), the emphatic form, which is usually accompanied by a verb of certainty, such as "you knew," "you verified," and "you were certain." Their fortresses were al-Wasm, al-Myda, al-Salalim, and al-Kathība.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: If you ask, what is the difference between your saying "And they thought that their fortresses would protect them" or "their protectors," and the arrangement in which it came? I say: fronting the predicate over the subject indicates their extreme confidence in its fortification and its protection of them. Making their pronoun the noun of *inna* and attributing the sentence to it indicates their belief about themselves that they were in might and protection, with which they would not care about anyone who attacked them or hoped to overpower them. That is not the case in your saying "And they thought that their fortresses would protect them." End of quotation. He means that *ḥuṣūnahum* is the subject and *māni'atuhum* is the predicate. This is not necessarily so. Rather, the preferred view is that *ḥuṣūnuhum* is the agent of *māni'atihim*, because his interpretation involves fronting and postponement, and permitting such a construction, such as *qā'imun Zaydun* (standing is Zayd) with Zayd as the subject and the predicate being the question, is disputed. The school of Kufa forbids it.

﴿So God came upon them﴾: that is, His punishment, ﴿from where they did not expect﴾: that is, it was not in their calculation. This was the killing of their chief, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. This was said by al-Suddī, Abū Ṣāliḥ, and Ibn Jurayj, and this weakened their strength.

﴿And He cast terror into their hearts﴾: He stripped their hearts of security and tranquility until they came down to the judgment of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

﴿They destroyed their houses with their own hands and the hands of the believers﴾. Qatādah said: The believers destroyed from the outside in order to enter, and they destroyed from the inside, and similar. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Zajjāj, and others said: Whenever the Muslims destroyed part of their fortresses, they demolished some of the houses, destroying the fortress. Al-Zuhrī and others said: When they were permitted to take what camels could carry, they left no good beam or pillar without tearing it out and destroying the houses around it. So His saying "and the hands of the believers" attributes the destruction to them, since the believers' siege of them was the cause of it. It was also said: They were stingy about leaving them intact, so they destroyed them out of corruption.

Qatādah, al-Jaḥdarī, Mujāhid, Abū Ḥaywa, 'Īsā, and Abū 'Amr read *wa-yukharribūna* with a doubled letter (intensive form). The rest of the seven read it without doubling. The two readings have one meaning: the intransitive *khariba* was made transitive by doubling and by the *hamza*. The author of *al-Kāmil fī al-qirā'āt* said: The doubled form is preferred for intensification. Abū 'Amr ibn al-'Alā' said: *kharraba* means demolished and corrupted, while *akhraba* means he left the place in ruins and went away from it.

﴿So take warning﴾: be alert to what God planned, by expelling them and giving the believers power over them without fighting.

It was also said: The Messenger of God ﷺ had promised the Muslims that God would give them their land and property without fighting, and he said, and it came to pass as he said.

﴿And had not God decreed for them exile, He would have punished them in this world﴾: that is, had He not decreed that He would expel them from their homes, and they would remain for a time, during which some of them would believe and some would have children who would believe, He would have punished them in this world with killing and captivity, as He did to their brothers, the Banū Qurayẓa. The Banū al-Naḍīr were among the army that disobeyed Moses, in that they did not kill (p. 244) the boy, son of the king of the Amalekites, leaving him for his camels and his intellect. Moses, peace be upon him, had said: Do not spare any of them. When they returned to Syria, they found that Moses, peace be upon him, had died. The Children of Israel said to them: You are disobedient. By God, you shall not enter our land. So they went away to the Ḥijāz and remained there. The exile that Bukht Naṣṣar inflicted on the people of Syria did not befall them. God had decreed exile upon the Children of Israel, so this exile befell them at the hand of Muḥammad ﷺ. Had it not been so, He would have punished them in this world with the sword and killing, like the people of Badr and others.

It is said: The people departed from their dwellings (*jalā*), and others expelled them (*ajlāhum*). It was said: The difference between *jalā'* and *ikhrāj* is that *jalā'* is when one leaves with family and children, while *ikhrāj* may occur with family and children remaining. Al-Māwardī said: *jalā'* occurs only for a group, while *ikhrāj* may occur for one person or a group. The majority read *al-jalā'* with a long vowel. Al-Ḥasan ibn Ṣāliḥ and his brother 'Alī ibn Ṣāliḥ read it short. Ṭalḥa read it with a *hamza* without an alif, like *al-naba'*.

﴿And for them in the Hereafter is the punishment of the Fire﴾: that is, if they escaped the punishment of this world, they will not escape in the Hereafter. Ṭalḥa read *wa-man yushāqiq* with clear pronunciation, like the consensus reading in al-Anfāl. The majority read it with assimilation (*idghām*).

Some of the Companions had begun to cut and burn some of the palm trees of the Banū al-Naḍīr, and that was at the start of the war. They said: What is this corruption, O Muḥammad, when you forbid corruption? So they stopped. Then this was revealed: ﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down or left standing on their roots, it was by God's permission﴾, to refute the Banū al-Naḍīr and to inform that this was by God's permission and enablement, so that He might disgrace you through it and humiliate you.

*Al-līna* and *al-nakhla* are two names with the same meaning, as said by al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, Ibn Zayd, and 'Amr ibn Maymūn. The poet said:

*As if my fetters above it were a bird's nest, upon a līna whose southern side flutters.*

Another said:

*A tawny dove sits upon a līna, its night-dew glistening on its feathers.*

Ibn 'Abbās and a group of lexicographers said: It is the palm tree as long as it is not 'ajwa (a kind of date). Al-Thawrī said: It is the noble palm tree. Abū 'Ubayda and Sufyān said: Its fruit is *lawn*, a kind of date called *al-lawn*. Sufyān said: It is very yellow, transparent so that its pit is seen from outside. Abū 'Ubayda also said: *al-līn* is the mixed varieties of palm trees among which there is no 'ajwa or barniyy. Ja'far ibn Muḥammad said: It is the 'ajwa. It was also said: It is the *sayalān* (a kind of date), and he cited for it:

*They planted līna in a flowing channel, then the palms were surrounded by thickets.*

It was also said: It is the branches of trees because of their softness, and in this case the *yā'* of the root is not a *wāw*. It was said: It is the short palm. Al-Aṣma'ī said: It is the *daql* (a kind of inferior date).

*Mā* here is conditional, in the accusative governed by *qaṭa'tum*, and *min līnatin* is a specification explaining the indefinite *mā*. The response of the condition is *fa-bi-idhni Allāh*, meaning: so whether He cut it or left it, it was by God's permission. The majority read *qā'imatan* with the feminine, agreeing with the sense of *mā*, and the pronoun in *tarktumūhā* refers to the sense of *mā*. 'Abd Allāh, al-A'mash, and Zayd ibn 'Alī read *qiwaman*, on the pattern *fi'al*, like *ḍirab*, as the plural of *qā'im*. It was also read *qā'iman* as an active participle, masculine according to the wording of *mā*, and feminine according to its meaning in *'alā uṣūlihā*. It was also read *uṣlihā* without a *wāw*.

When the Banū al-Naḍīr were expelled from their homelands and left their houses and wealth, the Muslims asked that it be divided into fifths, as with the spoils of Badr. Then this was revealed: ﴿Whatever God has bestowed (*afā'a*) upon His Messenger﴾. He explained that their wealth was *fay'* (booty without fighting), over which no horses or camels were driven, nor was any distance traveled. They were two miles from Medina, and they walked on foot, and only the Messenger of God rode. 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said: The wealth of the Banū al-Naḍīr belonged especially to the Messenger of God ﷺ. He spent from it on his family for the year's provision, then he put what remained into weapons and horses as a provision in the way of God, the Exalted. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: It was his, peace be upon him, and he gave it preference to the emigrants and distributed it among them, and he gave none of it to the Helpers except Abū Dujāna, Sahl ibn Ḥanīf, and al-Ḥārith ibn al-Ṣimma, whom he gave because of their poverty.

*Mā* in His saying ﴿whatever God bestowed upon His Messenger﴾ is conditional or relative. *Afā'a* is in the sense of *yafī'u* (future), and is not past in wording and meaning. For this reason, the relative clause of *mā* is with the *bā'* in its predicate, because it is then made similar to the conditional noun. If the verse was revealed before their expulsion, it was informing of the unseen, and it happened as it informed. If it was revealed after their wealth came to the Messenger ﷺ, it was an explanation of what would happen, and the ruling of the past preceding it is the same as its ruling. *Min* in ﴿from horses﴾ is extra in the object, indicated by the totality (*istighrāq*). *Rikāb* means camels. God gave His Messenger power over them and over what was in their hands, as He gave power to His messengers over whomever He wills of their enemies. Some scholars said: Everything that fell to the imams without being pursued by horses or camels belongs to them exclusively.

﴿Whatever God has bestowed upon His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾. Al-Zamakhsharī said: The conjunction is not used with this sentence, because it is an explanation of the first, so it is not foreign to it. It explained to the Messenger of God ﷺ what to do with what God had bestowed upon him, and commanded him to place it where one places the fifth of the spoils, divided into the five shares. End of quotation. Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: The people of the towns mentioned in this verse are the people of al-Ṣafrā', Yanbu', Wādī al-Qurā, and what is there of the towns of the Arabs called the towns of 'Urayna. Their ruling differs from the Banū al-Naḍīr, and the Messenger of God ﷺ did not withhold anything from these for himself, but gave them over to others, because they were conquered at that time. End of quotation. It was said: The first verse is specific to the Banū al-Naḍīr, and this verse is general.

The majority read ﴿so that it not be﴾ with *yā'*; 'Abd Allāh, Abū Ja'far, and Hishām read it with *tā'*. The majority read *dūlatan* with a *ḍamma* on the *dāl* and a *fatḥa* on the *tā'*; Abū Ja'far, Abū Ḥaywa, and Hishām read it with *ḍamma*; 'Alī and al-Sulamī read it with *fatḥa*. 'Īsā ibn 'Umar said: They have the same meaning. Al-Kisā'ī and the scholars of Basra said: The *fatḥa* is for the dynasty (*mulk*) with a *ḍamma* on the *mīm*, because it is the action of the age, and the *ḍamma* is for possession (*milk*) with a *kasra* on the *mīm*. The pronoun in *takūn* with the feminine refers to the sense of *mā*, since what is meant is the wealth and spoils, and that pronoun is the subject of *yakūn*. Likewise whoever read with *yā'* returned the pronoun to the wording of *mā*, meaning: that the *fay'* would be, and *dūlatan* is in the accusative as the predicate. Whoever read *dūlatun* in the nominative made *takūn* complete, and *dūlatun* the subject. And *kay lā yakūna* is a reason for His saying ﴿so to God and to the Messenger﴾, meaning: the *fay'* and its ruling belong to God and to the Messenger, who divides it as God the Exalted commanded, so that the *fay'*, whose due is to be given to the poor as a sustenance by which they live, will not circulate among the rich, who grow by it, or so that it will not become a pre-Islamic dynasty among them, as their chiefs used to monopolize the spoils and say: Whoever is mighty takes the best. The meaning: so that its taking is not by domination and pre-Islamic favoritism.

It is reported that some of the Helpers spoke about these conquered towns and said: We have our share of them. Then this was revealed: ﴿Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾. It is reported from al-Kalbī that some leaders of the Muslims said to him: O Messenger of God, take your *ṣafī* (choice portion) and the quarter, and leave us the rest, for thus we used to do in the pre-Islamic period. Then this was revealed: ﴿Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾, to the end of the verse. This is general, and it includes the division of what God bestowed as *fay'*, the spoils, and other things. So much so that this general wording has been used as evidence for the prohibition of wine, the ruling on the tattooed woman and the one who gets tattooed, and the prohibition of sewn garments for the one in ihram.

Among the strange anecdotes concerning istinbat (deduction of rulings) is that al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Ask me about whatever you wish, and I will inform you of it from the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of the Prophet (ﷺ)." Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Harun said to him: "What do you say about a muhrim (one in the state of ihram) who kills a *zunbur* (wasp)?" He replied: "Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾."

He related to us from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, from Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umayr, from Rib'i ibn Khirash, from Huthayfa ibn al-Yaman, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Follow those after me, Abu Bakr and Umar.'"

He related to us from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, from Mis'ar ibn Kidam, from Qays ibn Muslim, from Tariq ibn Shihab, from Umar ibn al-Khattab, that he ordered the killing of the *zunbur*. End of quotation. This means while in ihram.

He showed that Umar is to be followed, that the Messenger (ﷺ) ordered that he be followed, and that Allah the Exalted ordered the acceptance of what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) says.

[p. 246] His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿For the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes and their possessions, seeking bounty from Allah and His good pleasure, and supporting Allah and His Messenger. Those are the truthful.﴾ ﴿And those who had already settled in the abode and in faith before them love those who emigrate to them, and find in their breasts no need for what they have been given, and they prefer [them] over themselves, even though they themselves are in need. And whoever is protected from his own stinginess, those are the successful.﴾ ﴿And those who came after them say: "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and do not place in our hearts any rancour toward those who believe. Our Lord, You are indeed Compassionate and Merciful."﴾ ﴿Have you not considered those who played the hypocrite? They say to their brothers among the People of the Book who disbelieved: "If you are expelled, we will surely leave with you, and we will never obey anyone concerning you, and if you are fought against, we will surely support you." And Allah bears witness that they are indeed liars.﴾ ﴿If they are expelled, they will not leave with them; and if they are fought against, they will not support them; and if they do support them, they will surely turn their backs, then they will not be helped.﴾ ﴿Indeed, you are more fearful in their breasts than Allah. That is because they are a people who do not understand.﴾ ﴿They will not fight you all together except in fortified towns or from behind walls. Their violence among themselves is severe; you think them united, but their hearts are divided. That is because they are a people who do not reason.﴾

(For the poor) — al-Zamakhshari said: It is a badal (substitution, in grammatical terms an apposition/replacement) for His saying: (and to the near of kin). The conjoined element and what it is conjoined to, and the reason the substitution was not made from ﴿Allah's and the Messenger's﴾ [al-Anfal: 24], [p. 247] and what is conjoined to them both, even though the meaning is "for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)", is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, removed His Messenger from the poor by His saying: ﴿and they support Allah and His Messenger﴾, and that He elevates the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) above being named as "the poor," and that substitution according to the apparent wording contradicts what is obligatory in glorifying Allah, Mighty and Exalted. End of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari made it a substitution for His saying (and to the near of kin) only because it is the position of Abu Hanifa, and the meaning is that the near of kin deserves it only if he is poor. Poverty is thus a condition for him according to Abu Hanifa's view, and al-Zamakhshari interpreted it according to his school. As for al-Shafi'i, he holds that the cause of entitlement is kinship, so the near of kin receives it even if he is wealthy, because of his kinship.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿For the poor emigrants﴾ is an explanation of His saying: ﴿and the needy and the wayfarer﴾ [al-Hashr: 7]. The genitive preposition (lam) was repeated because the first one was governed by the lam, in order to distinguish between the wealthy among you, that is: but it is for the poor. End of quotation. Then Exalted is He described the emigrants with what indicates their poverty and necessitates compassion toward them.

﴿Those are the truthful﴾: that is, in their faith and their struggle, in word and in deed. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿And those who had already settled﴾ is conjoined to the emigrants, and they are the Helpers (al-Ansar), so there is a shared entitlement between them in what is distributed of the wealth. It has been said that it is a new independent sentence, nominative by inception, and the predicate is (they love). Allah Exalted praised them with these noble qualities, just as He praised the emigrants with His saying: ﴿seeking bounty﴾, etc. "And the faith" is conjoined to "the abode," which is Madina, and faith is not a place to be settled. It has been said that this is conjoining of sentences, that is: they held faith and were sincere in it. This was said by Abu 'Ali, and it is like his saying:

"I fed her chaff and cold water."

Or the meaning of "settling" includes the sense of "remaining," and remaining is a common element between the abode and faith, so the conjunction is valid. Or, since faith has encompassed them, it became like the place in which they dwell, but this would be a combination of the literal and the metaphorical. Al-Zamakhshari said: Or he intended the abode of emigration and the abode of faith, so he placed the definite article in "the abode" in place of the genitive, and omitted the head of "the abode of faith," and put the genitive in its place; or he named Madina because it is the abode of emigration and the place where faith became manifest through faith. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The meaning is that they settled in the abode together with faith, simultaneously, and by this combination the meaning of His saying (before them) is sound, so reflect on it. End of quotation. The meaning of (before them) is: before their emigration. (Need): that is, envy. ﴿from what they were given﴾: that is, from what was given to the emigrants. And what a need it was, that the Messenger (ﷺ) did in giving the emigrants from the wealth of the Banu al-Nadir and the [other] villages.

﴿And they prefer [them] over themselves﴾: among this is the story of the Ansari with the guest of the Messenger (ﷺ), when they had nothing but what the children eat; he gave the impression that he was eating, until the guest ate. The Messenger, peace be upon him, said: "Allah marvelled at what you both did last night." So the verse alludes to that. Other accounts of their preference have also been reported. Khasasa means poverty, derived from the khasas of the house, which is the gaps and openings that remain between its palm-stalks, so the condition of the poor is like that: deficiency and need penetrate it. Abu Haywa and Ibn Abi 'Abla read shiḥḥ with a kasra on the shin. The majority read it with a sukun on the waw, a light qaf and a damma on the shin. Shuhh means meanness, which is a tightness of the soul regarding what it possesses, and greed to withhold. The poet said:

"He wrestles a soul between his two sides, tight and stingy; when he intends to do good, it says to him: Wait."

The stinginess is attributed to the soul because it is an instinct within it. And He, Exalted, said: ﴿and souls are present with stinginess﴾ [al-Nisa': 128]. And in a hadith: "Whoever pays the obligatory zakat, hosts the guest, and gives in times of calamity, has been freed from stinginess."

﴿And those who came after them﴾: The apparent meaning is that it is conjoined to what precedes it of what is conjoined to the emigrants. Al-Farra' said: They are the third group of the Companions, namely whoever believed or disbelieved at the end of the Prophet's period (ﷺ). The majority said: He intended those who come from among the Successors. According to the first view, the meaning of (after them) is: after the emigrants and the earlier Helpers who preceded in faith, and these came later in their faith, or their faith preceded but their death was delayed until most of the emigrants and Helpers had passed away. According to the second view, the meaning of (after them) is: after the death of the emigrants, their emigrants and their helpers. If (and those who) is conjoined to the genitive noun before it, the apparent meaning is that they share with those mentioned earlier in the ruling of the fay' (spoils).

Malik ibn Aws said: 'Amr recited ﴿The alms are only for the poor﴾ [al-Tawba: 60], the verse, and said: "This is for these." Then he recited: ﴿And know that whatever you gain﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], and said: "And this is for these." Then he recited: ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger﴾ [al-Hashr: 7], until He reached ﴿for the poor emigrants﴾ up to ﴿And those who came after them﴾. Then he said: "If I live, I will surely give the shepherd his share of it while he is working [the land]." And also from him: that he consulted the emigrants and Helpers regarding what Allah had granted him from that, in much speech, the end of which was that he recited: ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger﴾ [al-Hashr: 7], the verse; when he reached ﴿Those are the truthful﴾ he said: "They are for these only," and he recited: ﴿And those who came after them﴾, the verse, up to His saying: (Compassionate, Merciful); then he said: "No one remains among the people of Islam except that he has entered into this." It has been said that ﴿And those who came after them﴾ is detached from what precedes it, conjoined as a conjunction of sentences, not a conjunction of single words; its i'rab (grammatical analysis) is: (And those who) is a subject (mubtada'), who were urged to supplicate for the earlier ones and praise them, and they are those who come after the Companions until the Day of Resurrection, and the predicate is (they say). Allah informed about them that, because of their faith and their love for their predecessors, ﴿they say: "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers"﴾. According to the first view, (they say) is a resumptive statement; it has been said, or it is a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿Have you not considered those who played the hypocrite﴾, the verse: It was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, Rifa'a ibn al-Tabut, and a group of the hypocrites of the Helpers, who had sent to the Banu al-Nadir what the reported sentences introduced by His saying (they say) contain. The lam in (to their brothers) is for conveying [the message], and the brotherhood between them is the brotherhood of disbelief and allegiance. ﴿and we will not obey you concerning [anything]﴾: that is, concerning your fighting, (anyone): from the Messenger and the believers; or ﴿we will not obey concerning you﴾: that is, concerning your abandonment and breaking what we promised you of support. And ﴿we will surely support you﴾ is the answer of an omitted oath before the conditional "in" (if), and the answer of "in" is omitted. The common usage in Arabic is to affirm the lam that signals an oath before the conditional particle, and an example of its omission is His saying: ﴿And if they do not desist from what they say, those who disbelieve among them will surely be touched﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 73]; the estimated meaning is: "And if they do not desist, they are indeed liars" — that is, in their promises to the Jews. This holds if (to their brothers) means that they were the Banu al-Nadir. It has been said that they were the Jews of Madina, and the pronouns follow these two views. It has been said that there is disagreement regarding them, that is: if the Jews are expelled, the hypocrites will not leave; if the Jews are fought, the hypocrites will not support them; if the hypocrites support the Jews, the Jews will turn their backs. It seems that the one who said this view looked at His saying: ﴿and if they are fought against, they will not support them﴾, since He informed that they will not support them, so how can ﴿and if they do support them﴾ come? So he placed it in the realm of possibility, while He had informed that they would not support them, so their supporting them after the information of Exalted Allah that it does not occur is impossible. When the pronouns are consistent, al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is "and if they support them" on the assumption, and the estimation is like His saying: ﴿If you associate [others with Allah], your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar: 65], and just as one knows what does not happen, if it were to happen, how it would be. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿they will surely turn their backs﴾, and in (then they will not be helped), refers to the supposed case that they support them, that is: and if the hypocrites support them, the hypocrites will surely turn their backs, then the hypocrites will not be helped. It has been said that the pronoun in turning back refers to the Jews, and likewise in (they will not be helped). Ibn 'Atiyya said: The verbs came without apocopation in His saying (they will not be expelled) and (they will not be helped), because they are governed by the rule of the oath, not by the rule of the condition; and in this there is room for consideration. End of quotation. And what consideration is there in this? This follows the established rule agreed upon: when the oath precedes the condition, the answer belongs to the oath and the answer of the condition is omitted, and its verb is in the past form or apocopated with lam; and it has a condition, which is that no demand for information precedes it. The lam in (la'in) signals an omitted oath before it, so the answer belongs to it. Al-Farra' permitted that the condition be answered even if the oath precedes it, but the Basrans rejected this against him. Then He addressed the believers: that these fear you with a fear more intense than [their fear of] Allah, Exalted, because they anticipate the immediate evil from you, and because of their lack of faith they do not anticipate the final punishment of Allah; and that is due to their little understanding. ﴿Rahba﴾ (fear) is a verbal noun of the passive form of rahiba, as if it were said: "more dreaded"; so the fear is from them, not from those addressed, and those addressed are feared. This is like the one who said:

"He is more to be feared in my view when I speak to him, though it is said that you are captive and slain.

From a lion in the wilderness of the earth, fearsome, in the hollow of 'Ithir, a thicket, beyond it a thicket."

So the one described is feared, not fearful. The pronoun in (their breasts) — it has been said: it refers to the Jews; it has been said: to the hypocrites; it has been said: to both groups. Making the breast a dwelling place for fear is evidence of its firm establishment among them, to the extent that the breasts became its dwelling place. The meaning is: their fear of you is greater than their fear of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿They will not fight you﴾: that is, the Banu al-Nadir and all the Jews. It was also said: the Jews and the hypocrites. ﴿All together﴾: that is, gathered and united, supporting one another, each strengthening the other. ﴿Except within fortified townships﴾: not in the open desert, out of their fear of you, and because they fortify them with trenches and ditches; or from behind a wall behind which they shelter themselves from being struck by you. Al-Jumhur read ﴿judur﴾ with two dammas, the plural of jidar (wall). Abu Raja, al-Hasan and Ibn Wathhab read it with the dal sukun for lightness; it is also reported from Ibn Kathir, Asim and al-A'mash. Abu Amr, Ibn Kathir and many of the Meccans read: jidar with an alif and a kasra on the jim. ﴿Their might among themselves is severe﴾: that is, when they fight one another, their might is severe. As for when they fight you, no strength remains to them, because whoever wars against the friends of God is forsaken.

﴿You think them to be united﴾: that is, gathered together, with bonds of affection and unity.

﴿But their hearts are divided﴾: that is, their desires are scattered. So too is the state of those who are forsaken; their desires do not settle upon one thing. [p. 246] His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿For the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes and their possessions, seeking bounty from Allah and His good pleasure, and supporting Allah and His Messenger. Those are the truthful.﴾ ﴿And those who had already settled in the abode and in faith before them love those who emigrate to them, and find in their breasts no need for what they have been given, and they prefer [them] over themselves, even though they themselves are in need. And whoever is protected from his own stinginess, those are the successful.﴾ ﴿And those who came after them say: "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and do not place in our hearts any rancour toward those who believe. Our Lord, You are indeed Compassionate and Merciful."﴾ ﴿Have you not considered those who played the hypocrite? They say to their brothers among the People of the Book who disbelieved: "If you are expelled, we will surely leave with you, and we will never obey anyone concerning you, and if you are fought against, we will surely support you." And Allah bears witness that they are indeed liars.﴾ ﴿If they are expelled, they will not leave with them; and if they are fought against, they will not support them; and if they do support them, they will surely turn their backs, then they will not be helped.﴾ ﴿Indeed, you are more fearful in their breasts than Allah. That is because they are a people who do not understand.﴾ ﴿They will not fight you all together except in fortified towns or from behind walls. Their violence among themselves is severe; you think them united, but their hearts are divided. That is because they are a people who do not reason.﴾

(For the poor) — al-Zamakhshari said: It is a badal (substitution, in grammatical terms an apposition/replacement) for His saying: (and to the near of kin). The conjoined element and what it is conjoined to, and the reason the substitution was not made from ﴿Allah's and the Messenger's﴾ [al-Anfal: 24], [p. 247] and what is conjoined to them both, even though the meaning is "for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)", is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, removed His Messenger from the poor by His saying: ﴿and they support Allah and His Messenger﴾, and that He elevates the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) above being named as "the poor," and that substitution according to the apparent wording contradicts what is obligatory in glorifying Allah, Mighty and Exalted. End of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari made it a substitution for His saying (and to the near of kin) only because it is the position of Abu Hanifa, and the meaning is that the near of kin deserves it only if he is poor. Poverty is thus a condition for him according to Abu Hanifa's view, and al-Zamakhshari interpreted it according to his school. As for al-Shafi'i, he holds that the cause of entitlement is kinship, so the near of kin receives it even if he is wealthy, because of his kinship.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿For the poor emigrants﴾ is an explanation of His saying: ﴿and the needy and the wayfarer﴾ [al-Hashr: 7]. The genitive preposition (lam) was repeated because the first one was governed by the lam, in order to distinguish between the wealthy among you, that is: but it is for the poor. End of quotation. Then Exalted is He described the emigrants with what indicates their poverty and necessitates compassion toward them.

﴿Those are the truthful﴾: that is, in their faith and their struggle, in word and in deed. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿And those who had already settled﴾ is conjoined to the emigrants, and they are the Helpers (al-Ansar), so there is a shared entitlement between them in what is distributed of the wealth. It has been said that it is a new independent sentence, nominative by inception, and the predicate is (they love). Allah Exalted praised them with these noble qualities, just as He praised the emigrants with His saying: ﴿seeking bounty﴾, etc. "And the faith" is conjoined to "the abode," which is Madina, and faith is not a place to be settled. It has been said that this is conjoining of sentences, that is: they held faith and were sincere in it. This was said by Abu 'Ali, and it is like his saying:

"I fed her chaff and cold water."

Or the meaning of "settling" includes the sense of "remaining," and remaining is a common element between the abode and faith, so the conjunction is valid. Or, since faith has encompassed them, it became like the place in which they dwell, but this would be a combination of the literal and the metaphorical. Al-Zamakhshari said: Or he intended the abode of emigration and the abode of faith, so he placed the definite article in "the abode" in place of the genitive, and omitted the head of "the abode of faith," and put the genitive in its place; or he named Madina because it is the abode of emigration and the place where faith became manifest through faith. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The meaning is that they settled in the abode together with faith, simultaneously, and by this combination the meaning of His saying (before them) is sound, so reflect on it. End of quotation. The meaning of (before them) is: before their emigration. (Need): that is, envy. ﴿from what they were given﴾: that is, from what was given to the emigrants. And what a need it was, that the Messenger (ﷺ) did in giving the emigrants from the wealth of the Banu al-Nadir and the [other] villages.

﴿And they prefer [them] over themselves﴾: among this is the story of the Ansari with the guest of the Messenger (ﷺ), when they had nothing but what the children eat; he gave the impression that he was eating, until the guest ate. The Messenger, peace be upon him, said: "Allah marvelled at what you both did last night." So the verse alludes to that. Other accounts of their preference have also been reported. Khasasa means poverty, derived from the khasas of the house, which is the gaps and openings that remain between its palm-stalks, so the condition of the poor is like that: deficiency and need penetrate it. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿they will surely turn their backs﴾, and in (then they will not be helped), refers to the supposed case that they support them, that is: and if the hypocrites support them, the hypocrites will surely turn their backs, then the hypocrites will not be helped. It has been said that the pronoun in turning back refers to the Jews, and likewise in (they will not be helped). Ibn 'Atiyya said: The verbs came without apocopation in His saying (they will not be expelled) and (they will not be helped), because they are governed by the rule of the oath, not by the rule of the condition; and in this there is room for consideration. End of quotation. And what consideration is there in this? This follows the established rule agreed upon: when the oath precedes the condition, the answer belongs to the oath and the answer of the condition is omitted, and its verb is in the past form or apocopated with lam; and it has a condition, which is that no demand for information precedes it. The lam in (la'in) signals an omitted oath before it, so the answer belongs to it. Al-Farra' permitted that the condition be answered even if the oath precedes it, but the Basrans rejected this against him. Then He addressed the believers: that these fear you with a fear more intense than [their fear of] Allah, Exalted, because they anticipate the immediate evil from you, and because of their lack of faith they do not anticipate the final punishment of Allah; and that is due to their little understanding. ﴿Rahba﴾ (fear) is a verbal noun of the passive form of rahiba, as if it were said: "more dreaded"; so the fear is from them, not from those addressed, and those addressed are feared. This is like the one who said:

"He is more to be feared in my view when I speak to him, though it is said that you are captive and slain.

From a lion in the wilderness of the earth, fearsome, in the hollow of 'Ithir, a thicket, beyond it a thicket."

So the one described is feared, not fearful. The pronoun in (their breasts) — it has been said: it refers to the Jews; it has been said: to the hypocrites; it has been said: to both groups. Making the breast a dwelling place for fear is evidence of its firm establishment among them, to the extent that the breasts became its dwelling place. The meaning is: their fear of you is greater than their fear of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿They will not fight you﴾: that is, the Banu al-Nadir and all the Jews. It was also said: the Jews and the hypocrites. ﴿All together﴾: that is, gathered and united, supporting one another, each strengthening the other. ﴿Except within fortified townships﴾: not in the open desert, out of their fear of you, and because they fortify them with trenches and ditches; or from behind a wall behind which they shelter themselves from being struck by you. Al-Jumhur read ﴿judur﴾ with two dammas, the plural of jidar (wall). Abu Raja, al-Hasan and Ibn Wathhab read it with the dal sukun for lightness; it is also reported from Ibn Kathir, Asim and al-A'mash. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿they will surely turn their backs﴾, and in (then they will not be helped), refers to the supposed case that they support them, that is: and if the hypocrites support them, the hypocrites will surely turn their backs, then the hypocrites will not be helped. It has been said that the pronoun in turning back refers to the Jews, and likewise in (they will not be helped). Ibn 'Atiyya said: The verbs came without apocopation in His saying (they will not be expelled) and (they will not be helped), because they are governed by the rule of the oath, not by the rule of the condition; and in this there is room for consideration. End of quotation. And what consideration is there in this? This follows the established rule agreed upon: when the oath precedes the condition, the answer belongs to the oath and the answer of the condition is omitted, and its verb is in the past form or apocopated with lam; and it has a condition, which is that no demand for information precedes it. The lam in (la'in) signals an omitted oath before it, so the answer belongs to it. Al-Farra' permitted that the condition be answered even if the oath precedes it, but the Basrans rejected this against him. Then He addressed the believers: that these fear you with a fear more intense than [their fear of] Allah, Exalted, because they anticipate the immediate evil from you, and because of their lack of faith they do not anticipate the final punishment of Allah; and that is due to their little understanding. ﴿Rahba﴾ (fear) is a verbal noun of the passive form of rahiba, as if it were said: "more dreaded"; so the fear is from them, not from those addressed, and those addressed are feared. This is like the one who said:

"He is more to be feared in my view when I speak to him, though it is said that you are captive and slain.

From a lion in the wilderness of the earth, fearsome, in the hollow of 'Ithir, a thicket, beyond it a thicket."

So the one described is feared, not fearful. The pronoun in (their breasts) — it has been said: it refers to the Jews; it has been said: to the hypocrites; it has been said: to both groups. Making the breast a dwelling place for fear is evidence of its firm establishment among them, to the extent that the breasts became its dwelling place. The meaning is: their fear of you is greater than their fear of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿They will not fight you﴾: that is, the Banu al-Nadir and all the Jews. It was also said: the Jews and the hypocrites. ﴿All together﴾: that is, gathered and united, supporting one another, each strengthening the other. ﴿Except within fortified townships﴾: not in the open desert, out of their fear of you, and because they fortify them with trenches and ditches; or from behind a wall behind which they shelter themselves from being struck by you. Al-Jumhur read ﴿judur﴾ with two dammas, the plural of jidar (wall). Abu Raja, al-Hasan and Ibn Wathhab read it with the dal sukun for lightness; it is also reported from Ibn Kathir, Asim and al-A'mash. Abu Amr, Ibn Kathir and many of the Meccans read: jidar with an alif and a kasra on the jim. Many of the Meccans and Harun, on the authority of Ibn Kathir, read: jadr, with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the dal. The author of al-Lawami said: this follows the dialect of Yemen. Ibn Atiyya said: its meaning is the base of a building, like a rampart or the like. He said: it may also be from jidr al-nakhl (the trunk/base of the palm), that is, from behind their palm trees, since these are used as a shield during close engagement.

﴿Their might among themselves is severe﴾: that is, when they fight one another, their might is severe. As for when they fight you, no strength remains to them, because whoever wars against the friends of God is forsaken.

﴿You think them to be united﴾: that is, gathered together, with bonds of affection and unity.

﴿But their hearts are divided﴾: that is, their desires are scattered. So too is the state of those who are forsaken; their desires do not settle upon one thing. The cause of that disunity is the absence of their intellects; they are like beasts that do not agree upon any one state. Al-Jumhur read ﴿shatta﴾ with the feminine alif; Mubashshir ibn Ubayd read it with tanwin, taking the alif as an alif of extension (ilhaq); Abdullah read: "wa qulubuhum ashatt," that is, more divided. From the speech of the Arabs: "shatta ta'uwibu al-halbah" (scattered, the milk-gathering returns to the same state...). The poet said:

"To God I complain of a band of youths who broke the staff of unity; today they are scattered, and yesterday they were united."

[p. 246] His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿For the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes and their possessions, seeking bounty from Allah and His good pleasure, and supporting Allah and His Messenger. Those are the truthful.﴾ ﴿And those who had already settled in the abode and in faith before them love those who emigrate to them, and find in their breasts no need for what they have been given, and they prefer [them] over themselves, even though they themselves are in need. And whoever is protected from his own stinginess, those are the successful.﴾ ﴿And those who came after them say: "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and do not place in our hearts any rancour toward those who believe. Our Lord, You are indeed Compassionate and Merciful."﴾ ﴿Have you not considered those who played the hypocrite? They say to their brothers among the People of the Book who disbelieved: "If you are expelled, we will surely leave with you, and we will never obey anyone concerning you, and if you are fought against, we will surely support you." And Allah bears witness that they are indeed liars.﴾ ﴿If they are expelled, they will not leave with them; and if they are fought against, they will not support them; and if they do support them, they will surely turn their backs, then they will not be helped.﴾ ﴿Indeed, you are more fearful in their breasts than Allah. That is because they are a people who do not understand.﴾ ﴿They will not fight you all together except in fortified towns or from behind walls. Their violence among themselves is severe; you think them united, but their hearts are divided. That is because they are a people who do not reason.﴾

(For the poor) — al-Zamakhshari said: It is a badal (substitution, in grammatical terms an apposition/replacement) for His saying: (and to the near of kin). The conjoined element and what it is conjoined to, and the reason the substitution was not made from ﴿Allah's and the Messenger's﴾ [al-Anfal: 24], [p. 247] and what is conjoined to them both, even though the meaning is "for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)", is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, removed His Messenger from the poor by His saying: ﴿and they support Allah and His Messenger﴾, and that He elevates the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) above being named as "the poor," and that substitution according to the apparent wording contradicts what is obligatory in glorifying Allah, Mighty and Exalted. End of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari made it a substitution for His saying (and to the near of kin) only because it is the position of Abu Hanifa, and the meaning is that the near of kin deserves it only if he is poor. Poverty is thus a condition for him according to Abu Hanifa's view, and al-Zamakhshari interpreted it according to his school. As for al-Shafi'i, he holds that the cause of entitlement is kinship, so the near of kin receives it even if he is wealthy, because of his kinship.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿For the poor emigrants﴾ is an explanation of His saying: ﴿and the needy and the wayfarer﴾ [al-Hashr: 7]. The genitive preposition (lam) was repeated because the first one was governed by the lam, in order to distinguish between the wealthy among you, that is: but it is for the poor. End of quotation. Then Exalted is He described the emigrants with what indicates their poverty and necessitates compassion toward them.

﴿Those are the truthful﴾: that is, in their faith and their struggle, in word and in deed. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿And those who had already settled﴾ is conjoined to the emigrants, and they are the Helpers (al-Ansar), so there is a shared entitlement between them in what is distributed of the wealth. It has been said that it is a new independent sentence, nominative by inception, and the predicate is (they love). Allah Exalted praised them with these noble qualities, just as He praised the emigrants with His saying: ﴿seeking bounty﴾, etc. "And the faith" is conjoined to "the abode," which is Madina, and faith is not a place to be settled. It has been said that this is conjoining of sentences, that is: they held faith and were sincere in it. This was said by Abu 'Ali, and it is like his saying:

"I fed her chaff and cold water."

Or the meaning of "settling" includes the sense of "remaining," and remaining is a common element between the abode and faith, so the conjunction is valid. Or, since faith has encompassed them, it became like the place in which they dwell, but this would be a combination of the literal and the metaphorical. Al-Zamakhshari said: Or he intended the abode of emigration and the abode of faith, so he placed the definite article in "the abode" in place of the genitive, and omitted the head of "the abode of faith," and put the genitive in its place; or he named Madina because it is the abode of emigration and the place where faith became manifest through faith. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The meaning is that they settled in the abode together with faith, simultaneously, and by this combination the meaning of His saying (before them) is sound, so reflect on it. End of quotation. The meaning of (before them) is: before their emigration. (Need): that is, envy. ﴿from what they were given﴾: that is, from what was given to the emigrants. And what a need it was, that the Messenger (ﷺ) did in giving the emigrants from the wealth of the Banu al-Nadir and the [other] villages.

﴿And they prefer [them] over themselves﴾: among this is the story of the Ansari with the guest of the Messenger (ﷺ), when they had nothing but what the children eat; he gave the impression that he was eating, until the guest ate. The Messenger, peace be upon him, said: "Allah marvelled at what you both did last night." So the verse alludes to that. Other accounts of their preference have also been reported. Khasasa means poverty, derived from the khasas of the house, which is the gaps and openings that remain between its palm-stalks, so the condition of the poor is like that: deficiency and need penetrate it. Abu Haywa and Ibn Abi 'Abla read shiḥḥ with a kasra on the shin. The majority read it with a sukun on the waw, a light qaf and a damma on the shin. Shuhh means meanness, which is a tightness of the soul regarding what it possesses, and greed to withhold. The poet said:

"He wrestles a soul between his two sides, tight and stingy; when he intends to do good, it says to him: Wait."

The stinginess is attributed to the soul because it is an instinct within it. And He, Exalted, said: ﴿and souls are present with stinginess﴾ [al-Nisa': 128]. And in a hadith: "Whoever pays the obligatory zakat, hosts the guest, and gives in times of calamity, has been freed from stinginess."

﴿And those who came after them﴾: The apparent meaning is that it is conjoined to what precedes it of what is conjoined to the emigrants. Al-Farra' said: They are the third group of the Companions, namely whoever believed or disbelieved at the end of the Prophet's period (ﷺ). The majority said: He intended those who come from among the Successors. According to the first view, the meaning of (after them) is: after the emigrants and the earlier Helpers who preceded in faith, and these came later in their faith, or their faith preceded but their death was delayed until most of the emigrants and Helpers had passed away. According to the second view, the meaning of (after them) is: after the death of the emigrants, their emigrants and their helpers. If (and those who) is conjoined to the genitive noun before it, the apparent meaning is that they share with those mentioned earlier in the ruling of the fay' (spoils).

Malik ibn Aws said: 'Amr recited ﴿The alms are only for the poor﴾ [al-Tawba: 60], the verse, and said: "This is for these." Then he recited: ﴿And know that whatever you gain﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], and said: "And this is for these." Then he recited: ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger﴾ [al-Hashr: 7], until He reached ﴿for the poor emigrants﴾ up to ﴿And those who came after them﴾. Then he said: "If I live, I will surely give the shepherd his share of it while he is working [the land]." And also from him: that he consulted the emigrants and Helpers regarding what Allah had granted him from that, in much speech, the end of which was that he recited: ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger﴾ [al-Hashr: 7], the verse; when he reached ﴿Those are the truthful﴾ he said: "They are for these only," and he recited: ﴿And those who came after them﴾, the verse, up to His saying: (Compassionate, Merciful); then he said: "No one remains among the people of Islam except that he has entered into this." And 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Were it not for those who come from the last of the people, I would not conquer a village except that I would divide it as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) divided Khaybar." It has been said that ﴿And those who came after them﴾ is detached from what precedes it, conjoined as a conjunction of sentences, not a conjunction of single words; its i'rab (grammatical analysis) is: (And those who) is a subject (mubtada'), who were urged to supplicate for the earlier ones and praise them, and they are those who come after the Companions until the Day of Resurrection, and the predicate is (they say). Allah informed about them that, because of their faith and their love for their predecessors, ﴿they say: "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers"﴾. According to the first view, (they say) is a resumptive statement; it has been said, or it is a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿Have you not considered those who played the hypocrite﴾, the verse: It was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, Rifa'a ibn al-Tabut, and a group of the hypocrites of the Helpers, who had sent to the Banu al-Nadir what the reported sentences introduced by His saying (they say) contain. The lam in (to their brothers) is for conveying [the message], and the brotherhood between them is the brotherhood of disbelief and allegiance. ﴿and we will not obey you concerning [anything]﴾: that is, concerning your fighting, (anyone): from the Messenger and the believers; or ﴿we will not obey concerning you﴾: that is, concerning your abandonment and breaking what we promised you of support. And ﴿we will surely support you﴾ is the answer of an omitted oath before the conditional "in" (if), and the answer of "in" is omitted. The common usage in Arabic is to affirm the lam that signals an oath before the conditional particle, and an example of its omission is His saying: ﴿And if they do not desist from what they say, those who disbelieve among them will surely be touched﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 73]; the estimated meaning is: "And if they do not desist, they are indeed liars" — that is, in their promises to the Jews. In that is evidence for the validity of prophethood, because it is information about the unseen, and for that reason they did not leave when the Banu al-Nadir were expelled; rather they remained in their homes. This holds if (to their brothers) means that they were the Banu al-Nadir. It has been said that they were the Jews of Madina, and the pronouns follow these two views. It has been said that there is disagreement regarding them, that is: if the Jews are expelled, the hypocrites will not leave; if the Jews are fought, the hypocrites will not support them; if the hypocrites support the Jews, the Jews will turn their backs. It seems that the one who said this view looked at His saying: ﴿and if they are fought against, they will not support them﴾, since He informed that they will not support them, so how can ﴿and if they do support them﴾ come? So he placed it in the realm of possibility, while He had informed that they would not support them, so their supporting them after the information of Exalted Allah that it does not occur is impossible. When the pronouns are consistent, al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is "and if they support them" on the assumption, and the estimation is like His saying: ﴿If you associate [others with Allah], your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar: 65], and just as one knows what does not happen, if it were to happen, how it would be. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The meaning is: and if they oppose that, then they will be defeated. End of quotation. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿they will surely turn their backs﴾, and in (then they will not be helped), refers to the supposed case that they support them, that is: and if the hypocrites support them, the hypocrites will surely turn their backs, then the hypocrites will not be helped. It has been said that the pronoun in turning back refers to the Jews, and likewise in (they will not be helped). Ibn 'Atiyya said: The verbs came without apocopation in His saying (they will not be expelled) and (they will not be helped), because they are governed by the rule of the oath, not by the rule of the condition; and in this there is room for consideration. End of quotation. And what consideration is there in this? This follows the established rule agreed upon: when the oath precedes the condition, the answer belongs to the oath and the answer of the condition is omitted, and its verb is in the past form or apocopated with lam; and it has a condition, which is that no demand for information precedes it. The lam in (la'in) signals an omitted oath before it, so the answer belongs to it. Al-Farra' permitted that the condition be answered even if the oath precedes it, but the Basrans rejected this against him. Then He addressed the believers: that these fear you with a fear more intense than [their fear of] Allah, Exalted, because they anticipate the immediate evil from you, and because of their lack of faith they do not anticipate the final punishment of Allah; and that is due to their little understanding. ﴿Rahba﴾ (fear) is a verbal noun of the passive form of rahiba, as if it were said: "more dreaded"; so the fear is from them, not from those addressed, and those addressed are feared. This is like the one who said:

"He is more to be feared in my view when I speak to him, though it is said that you are captive and slain.

From a lion in the wilderness of the earth, fearsome, in the hollow of 'Ithir, a thicket, beyond it a thicket."

So the one described is feared, not fearful. The pronoun in (their breasts) — it has been said: it refers to the Jews; it has been said: to the hypocrites; it has been said: to both groups. Making the breast a dwelling place for fear is evidence of its firm establishment among them, to the extent that the breasts became its dwelling place. The meaning is: their fear of you is greater than their fear of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿They will not fight you﴾: that is, the Banu al-Nadir and all the Jews. It was also said: the Jews and the hypocrites. ﴿All together﴾: that is, gathered and united, supporting one another, each strengthening the other. ﴿Except within fortified townships﴾: not in the open desert, out of their fear of you, and because they fortify them with trenches and ditches; or from behind a wall behind which they shelter themselves from being struck by you. Al-Jumhur read ﴿judur﴾ with two dammas, the plural of jidar (wall). Abu Raja, al-Hasan and Ibn Wathhab read it with the dal sukun for lightness; it is also reported from Ibn Kathir, Asim and al-A'mash. Abu Amr, Ibn Kathir and many of the Meccans read: jidar with an alif and a kasra on the jim. Many of the Meccans and Harun, on the authority of Ibn Kathir, read: jadr, with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the dal. The author of al-Lawami said: this follows the dialect of Yemen. Ibn Atiyya said: its meaning is the base of a building, like a rampart or the like. He said: it may also be from jidr al-nakhl (the trunk/base of the palm), that is, from behind their palm trees, since these are used as a shield during close engagement.

﴿Their might among themselves is severe﴾: that is, when they fight one another, their might is severe. As for when they fight you, no strength remains to them, because whoever wars against the friends of God is forsaken.

﴿You think them to be united﴾: that is, gathered together, with bonds of affection and unity.

﴿But their hearts are divided﴾: that is, their desires are scattered. So too is the state of those who are forsaken; their desires do not settle upon one thing. The cause of that disunity is the absence of their intellects; they are like beasts that do not agree upon any one state. Al-Jumhur read ﴿shatta﴾ with the feminine alif; Mubashshir ibn Ubayd read it with tanwin, taking the alif as an alif of extension (ilhaq); Abdullah read: "wa qulubuhum ashatt," that is, more divided. From the speech of the Arabs: "shatta ta'uwibu al-halbah" (scattered, the milk-gathering returns to the same state...). The poet said:

"To God I complain of a band of youths who broke the staff of unity; today they are scattered, and yesterday they were united."

(p. 250) *kamathali* (كَمَثَلِ): the predicate of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*), meaning "their case is like..." i.e., the Banu an-Nadir. ﴿Like those before them, shortly before: they tasted the consequence of their affair, and for them there is a painful punishment.﴾ Those before them are the Banu Qaynuqa', whom the Messenger (ﷺ) expelled from Madina before the Banu an-Nadir, so they were an example for them, as said by Ibn 'Abbas. Or they are the disbelievers of Badr, whom the Prophet (ﷺ) killed, so they are like them in being defeated and subdued. It is also said that the pronoun in *min qablihim* refers to the hypocrites, and *alladhina min qablihim* means the hypocrites of earlier nations, who were defeated and humiliated throughout time, so these are like them. This interpretation is weakened by the word *qarifan* (قَرِيبًا) if you make it dependent on what precedes it. If *qarifan* is a time adverb (*zarf zaman*) and you make it an object of *dhaqu* (ذاقُوا), then the meaning is: they tasted the consequence of their affair shortly after their disobedience, i.e., their punishment was not delayed in this world, just as the punishment of those was not delayed. ﴿And for them there is a painful punishment﴾ in the Hereafter.

﴿Like the Shaytan﴾: Having compared them to those before them, he mentioned their likeness to the hypocrites. The hypocrites are like Satan, and the Banu an-Nadir are like the human. The majority hold that *ash-shaytan* and *al-insan* are generic nouns (*ism jins*): he draws him into disobedience and then flees from him. Likewise the hypocrites misled the Banu an-Nadir, encouraged them to stand firm, and promised them victory. When the Banu an-Nadir were caught, the hypocrites abandoned them and left them in the worst condition. It is also said that what is meant is Satan's seducing of the Quraysh on the Day of Badr, and his saying to them: ﴿No one among the people will overcome you today, and I am your protector﴾ [al-Anfal: 48], up to his saying: ﴿Indeed, I am free of you﴾ [al-Anfal: 48]. It is also said that the comparison is with a specific devil and a specific worshipper who was entrusted with a woman. He had intercourse with her and she became pregnant, so he feared disgrace and killed her and buried her. Satan made that seem fine to him, then exposed him, and she was dug up and found murdered. He had said that she had died and that he had buried her, so they learned the truth. Satan then confronted him and said: "Disbelieve and prostrate to me, and I will save you." He did so, and then at that point Satan left him and said: "I am free of you." Satan's saying ﴿Indeed, I fear Allah﴾ is mere show, and his fear does not prevent him from the evil into which he drags the son of Adam.

The majority read *'aqibatahuma* (عاقِبَتَهُما) with a fatha on the *ta'*. Al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and Salim ibn Arqam read it with a damma on the *ta'*. The majority read *khalidayn* (خالِدِينَ) with *ya'* as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), and *fi an-nar* (في النّارِ) as the predicate of *inna*. 'Abdullah, Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-A'mash and Ibn 'Abla read it with *alif*, so it may be the predicate of *inna*, and the adverbial phrase is then cancelled (*mulgha*), even though it is emphasised by his saying *fiha* (فِيها). This is permissible according to the school of Sibawayh, but the people of Kufa prohibited it, because when it is emphasised according to them, it is not cancelled. It is also possible that *fi an-nar* is the predicate, since *khalidin* is a second predicate, and then there is no proof in it according to the school of Sibawayh.

When the description of the hypocrites and the Jews ended in this surah, he exhorted the believers, because admonition after mention of a calamity has an effect on the soul, due to the softness of hearts and the caution against what brings punishment. He repeated the command to piety for emphasis, or because the object of piety differs. The first is in performing the obligations, because it is linked to action; the second is in abstaining from sins, because it is linked to threat and warning. The majority read *wal-tanzur* (ولْتَنْظُرْ) as a command with a silent *lam*; Abu Haywa and Yahya ibn al-Harith read it with a *kasra* on the *lam*, which is also reported from Hafs from 'Asim. Al-Hasan read it with a *kasra* on the *lam* and a fatha on the *ra'*, making it a *lam* of purpose (*lam kay*). Since the matter of the Resurrection is certain to happen, he referred to it as "tomorrow," which is the day that follows your day, by way of approximation. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: he has not ceased to affirm it until he made it like tomorrow. A similar usage is ﴿as if it had not flourished yesterday﴾ [Yunus: 24], meaning the bringing near of past time. It is also said that he referred to the Hereafter as "tomorrow," as if this world and the Hereafter were two days: a day and a tomorrow. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it may also mean by his saying ﴿for tomorrow﴾ the day of death, since for every person it is like his tomorrow. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: "yesterday" is this world and "tomorrow" is the Hereafter. Al-Zamakhshari said: as for indefinite *nafs* (نَفْسٌ), it signifies the minimizing of the souls that look at what they have sent forward for the Hereafter, as if it were said: for a tomorrow whose reality is unknown because of its greatness. End of quote. The majority read *la takunu* (لا تَكُونُوا) with the *ta'* of address; Abu Haywa read it with the *ya'* of the third person, as a shift of person (*iltifat*).

Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is an allusion to *nafs*, which is a generic noun. ﴿Like those who forgot﴾: they are the disbelievers, who abandoned the worship of Allah, the carrying out of what He commanded, and the avoidance of what He forbade. This points to the extreme of their heedlessness and their following of their desires. ﴿So He caused them to forget themselves﴾, since they did not strive for their own deliverance from punishment. This is a case of requital for sin with sin: they were punished for forgetting the right of Allah by having Him cause them to forget themselves. Sufyan said: the meaning is the share of their own souls. Then he mentioned the contrast between the two groups: the people of the Fire are in the blazing hell, and the people of Paradise are in bliss, as He said: ﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was defiantly disobedient? They are not equal﴾ [al-Sajda: 18], and He said: ﴿Or shall We treat the righteous like the wicked?﴾ [Sad: 28].

﴿If We had sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain﴾: this is by way of imagination and representation (*takhyil wa tamthil*), as mentioned in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We offered the trust to the heavens﴾ [al-Ahzab: 72]. What points to this is ﴿And these are the parables We present to the people﴾. The purpose is to rebuke the human for the hardness of his heart and for his lack of being affected by this, since if it were sent down upon a mountain it would humble itself and split apart. If the mountain, despite its greatness and hardness, is subject to humility and splitting, the son of Adam is more deserving of that, yet despite his insignificance and weakness he is not affected. Talha read *musaddi'an* (مُصَّدِّعًا) with the *ta'* assimilated into the *sad*. Abu as-Sammal and Abu Dinar al-A'rabi read *al-Quddus* (القَدُّوسُ) with a fatha on the *qaf*; the majority read it with a fatha on the *qaf* and a damma on the *dal*. Al-Zamakhshari said: as for indefinite *nafs* (نَفْسٌ), it signifies the minimizing of the souls that look at what they have sent forward for the Hereafter, as if it were said: for a tomorrow whose reality is unknown because of its greatness. End of quote. The majority read *la takunu* (لا تَكُونُوا) with the *ta'* of address; Abu Haywa read it with the *ya'* of the third person, as a shift of person (*iltifat*).

Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is an allusion to *nafs*, which is a generic noun. ﴿Like those who forgot﴾: they are the disbelievers, who abandoned the worship of Allah, the carrying out of what He commanded, and the avoidance of what He forbade. This points to the extreme of their heedlessness and their following of their desires. ﴿So He caused them to forget themselves﴾, since they did not strive for their own deliverance from punishment. This is a case of requital for sin with sin: they were punished for forgetting the right of Allah by having Him cause them to forget themselves. Sufyan said: the meaning is the share of their own souls. Then he mentioned the contrast between the two groups: the people of the Fire are in the blazing hell, and the people of Paradise are in bliss, as He said: ﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was defiantly disobedient? They are not equal﴾ [al-Sajda: 18], and He said: ﴿Or shall We treat the righteous like the wicked?﴾ [Sad: 28].

﴿If We had sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain﴾: this is by way of imagination and representation (*takhyil wa tamthil*), as mentioned in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We offered the trust to the heavens﴾ [al-Ahzab: 72]. What points to this is ﴿And these are the parables We present to the people﴾. The purpose is to rebuke the human for the hardness of his heart and for his lack of being affected by this, since if it were sent down upon a mountain it would humble itself and split apart. If the mountain, despite its greatness and hardness, is subject to humility and splitting, the son of Adam is more deserving of that, yet despite his insignificance and weakness he is not affected. Talha read *musaddi'an* (مُصَّدِّعًا) with the *ta'* assimilated into the *sad*. Abu as-Sammal and Abu Dinar al-A'rabi read *al-Quddus* (القَدُّوسُ) with a fatha on the *qaf*; the majority read it with a fatha on the *qaf* and a damma on the *dal*. The majority read *al-Mu'min* (المُؤْمِنُ) with a *kasra* on the *mim*, as an active participle from *amana*, in the sense of *amman* (granting security). Tha'lab said: the one who confirms the believers in that they have believed. Al-Nahhas said: or in His testimony over people on the Day of Resurrection. It is also said: the one who confirms Himself in His eternal sayings. Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, and it is said Abu Ja'far al-Madani, read *al-Mu'man* (المُؤْمَنُ) with a fatha on the *mim*. Abu Hatim said: this is not permissible, because if it were so it would be "*al-mu'man bihi*" and that would be allowed, but the unrestricted *al-mu'man* without a preposition refers to one who was fearful and then given security. Al-Zamakhshari said: he means *al-mu'man bihi* with the preposition omitted, just as you say of the people of Musa, from His saying ﴿And Musa chose his people﴾ [al-A'raf: 155]: "the chosen ones" (*al-mukhtarun*).

﴿Al-Muhaymin﴾: its explanation has already passed.

﴿Al-Jabbar﴾: the Subduer who compelled His creation to what He willed. It is also said: *al-Jabbar* is the one to whom nothing comes close and who cannot be reached, and from this comes *nakhla jabbara* (a palm tree) when it cannot be reached. Imru' al-Qays said:

*Tall palms, the lofty one whose branches are thick,*
*and bearing clusters of red unripe dates.*
